{{short description|Function space of all functions whose derivatives are rapidly decreasing}}
{{for multi|the Schwartz space of a semisimple Lie group|Harish-Chandra's Schwartz space|the Schwartz space of a locally compact abelian group|Schwartz–Bruhat function}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Schwartz space <math>\mathcal{S}</math>''' is the [[function space]] of all [[Function (mathematics)|functions]] whose [[derivative]]s of all orders are [[Vanish_at_infinity#Rapidly_decreasing|rapidly decreasing]].  This space has the important property that the [[Fourier transform]] is an [[automorphism]] on this space. This property enables one, by duality, to define the Fourier transform for elements in the dual space <math>\mathcal{S}^*</math> of {{tmath| \mathcal{S} }}, that is, for [[tempered distributions]].  A function in the Schwartz space is sometimes called a '''Schwartz function'''.
[[File:Gaussian 2D.png|right|thumb|250px|A two-dimensional [[Gaussian function]] is an example of a rapidly decreasing function.]]

Schwartz space is named after French mathematician [[Laurent Schwartz]].

== Definition ==

Let <math>\mathbb{N}</math> be the [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of non-negative [[integer]]s, and for any {{tmath| n \in \mathbb{N} }}, let <math>\mathbb{N}^n := \underbrace{\mathbb{N} \times \dots \times \mathbb{N}}_{n \text{ times}}</math> be the {{tmath| n }}-fold [[Cartesian product]]. 

The ''Schwartz space'' or '''space of rapidly decreasing functions on''' <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> is the function space<math display="block">\mathcal{S} \left(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{C}\right) := \left \{ f \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{C}) \mid \forall \boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathbb{N}^n, \|f\|_{\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}}< \infty\right \},</math> where <math>C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{C})</math> is the function space of [[smooth function]]s from <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> into {{tmath| \mathbb{C} }}, and <math display="block">\|f\|_{\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}}:= \sup_{\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n} \left| \boldsymbol{x}^\boldsymbol{\alpha} (\boldsymbol{D}^\boldsymbol{\beta} f)(\boldsymbol{x}) \right|.</math> Here, <math>\sup</math> denotes the [[supremum]], and we used [[multi-index notation]], i.e. <math>\boldsymbol{x}^\boldsymbol{\alpha} := x_1^{\alpha_1}x_2^{\alpha_2}\ldots x_n^{\alpha_n}</math> and {{tmath|1= D^\boldsymbol{\beta} := \partial_1^{\beta_1}\partial_2^{\beta_2}\ldots \partial_n^{\beta_n} }}.

To put common language to this definition, one could consider a rapidly decreasing function as essentially a function <math>f</math> such that {{tmath| f(x) }}, {{tmath| f'(x) }}, {{tmath| f^{\prime\prime}(x) }}, ... all exist everywhere on <math>\mathbb{R}</math> and go to zero as <math>x \rightarrow \pm \infty</math> faster than any reciprocal power of {{tmath| x }}. In particular, <math>\mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{C}\right)</math> is a [[Linear subspace|subspace]] of {{tmath| C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathbb{C}) }}.

== Examples of functions in the Schwartz space ==
* If <math>\boldsymbol{\alpha}</math> is a multi-index, and ''a'' is a positive [[real number]], then {{tmath| \boldsymbol{x}^\boldsymbol{\alpha} e^{-a \vert \boldsymbol{x} \vert^2} \in \mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^n) }}.
* Any smooth function <math>f</math> with [[compact support]] is in {{tmath| \mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right) }}. This is clear since any derivative of <math>f</math> is [[Continuous function|continuous]] and supported in the support of {{tmath| f }}, so <math>(\boldsymbol{x}^\boldsymbol{\alpha}\boldsymbol{D}^\boldsymbol{\alpha})f</math> has a maximum in <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> by the [[extreme value theorem]].
* Because the Schwartz space is a vector space, any polynomial <math>\phi(\boldsymbol{x})</math> can be multiplied by a factor <math> e^{-a \vert\boldsymbol{x}\vert^2}</math> for <math>a > 0</math> a real constant, to give an element of the Schwartz space. In particular, there is an embedding of polynomials into a Schwartz space.

== Properties ==

=== Analytic properties ===
* From [[General Leibniz rule|Leibniz's rule]], it follows that <math>\mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)</math> is also closed under [[Pointwise product|pointwise multiplication]]: {{tmath| f, g \in \mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right) }} implies {{tmath| fg \in \mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right) }}. In particular, this implies that <math>\mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)</math> is an <math>\mathbb{R}</math>-algebra. More generally, if <math>f \in\mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}\right)</math> and <math>H</math> is a bounded smooth function with bounded derivatives of all orders, then {{tmath| fH \in\mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}\right) }}.
* The Fourier transform is a [[linear isomorphism]] {{tmath| \mathcal F:\mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right) \rightarrow \mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right) }}.
* If <math>f \in \mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)</math> then <math>f</math> is [[Lipschitz continuous]] and hence [[uniformly continuous]] on {{tmath| \mathbb{R}^n }}.
* <math>\mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)</math> is a [[Distinguished space|distinguished]] [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] [[Fréchet space|Fréchet]] [[Schwartz topological vector space|Schwartz TVS]] over the [[complex number]]s.
* Both <math>\mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)</math> '''''and''''' its [[strong dual space]] are also:
# [[Complete topological vector space|complete]] [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] [[Locally convex topological vector space|locally convex]] spaces,
# [[Nuclear space|nuclear]] [[Montel space]]s,
<!-- ::It is known that in the [[Continuous dual space|dual space]] of any Montel space, a sequence converges in the [[Strong dual space|strong dual topology]] if and only if it converges in the [[weak* topology]].{{sfn | Trèves | 2006 | pp=351–359}} - Relevance to this entry? This rather belongs to [[Montel space]] -->
# [[ultrabornological space]]s,
# [[Reflexive space|reflexive]] [[Barrelled space|barrelled]] [[Mackey space]]s.

=== Relation of Schwartz spaces with other topological vector spaces ===
* If {{tmath| 1 \leqslant p < \infty }}, then <math>\mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right)</math> is a [[Dense set|dense]] subset of {{tmath| L^p(\mathbb{R}^n) }}.
* The space of all [[bump function]]s, {{tmath| C_\text{c}^\infty\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right) }}, is included in {{tmath| \mathcal{S}\left(\mathbb{R}^n\right) }}.
